# Access

Roles, capabilities with field lists and row filters, field rules, anonymous access, and what they default to.

Roles are defined in code ([`defineRoles`](https://docs.protobase.net/api/schema/functions/defineroles/))) and assigned through the auth user's `roles`; with [organizations](auth.md#organizations)), also per membership, and `ctx.user.roles` holds both, while `ctx.organization.id` is the organization the request works in. Rules decide per operation (`list`, `read`, `create`, `update`, `delete`), per field (role-based, never per record) and per row (filters, like RLS).

## Defaults

- A project that passes `roles` to `resolveAccess` is **default deny**: an operation without a rule needs the capability `<resource>.<action>` (`list` uses `read`), so admin's `*` still passes. A field without a rule follows its resource.
- A project without roles (the single-admin case) is **default allow**.
- `defaultAccess: 'allow'` together with `roles` is an explicit opt-in. Print `accessWarnings(options)` at startup.
- Every request needs a token, unless the roles define [`anonymous`](#anonymous-access).
- An [API function](../guides/api-functions.md#roles)) without `roles` or a `capability` is closed the same way: with roles, only a caller holding `*` may call it.

## Capabilities

A role is a list of capabilities, `<resource|area>.<action>[.<scope>]`: `orders.read`, `orders.update.own`, `costs.read` (an area, for field rules), `*.read` or `*`. An entry may also be an object that limits capabilities to fields, rows or both:

```ts
defineRoles<'orders' | 'products'>({
  sales: ['orders.read.own', 'orders.create', 'products.read'],
  erp_sync: [{ 'products.read': ['sku', 'price', 'stock'] }, { 'products.update': ['stock'] }],
  reseller: [{ 'products.read': { fields: ['sku', 'name', 'price'], filter: 'published = true' } }],
})
```

- **Fields** (`['sku', 'price']`, or `fields` in an object) are an allowlist: for `<resource>.read`, `.create` or `.update`, the role reads or writes only the fields listed, so a column added later stays hidden from it until someone lists it. Key columns are always there, because records are addressed by them. A plain capability (`'products.read'`) still means every field.
- **Filter** is AIP-160 text, like a filter an access rule returns. It narrows the rows of the capability, together with `.own` or `.team` when the capability has one.
- A limit names one resource, never `*`, and fields go with `read`, `create` or `update` only; `defineRoles` refuses anything else. At startup the server refuses a field the resource does not have, a filter that does not fit it, and a limit on a name that is not a resource.

A field is readable when the role's list allows it and the field's own [rule](#field-rules-or-field-lists) passes. Field lists take effect through the roles the server gets (`options: { roles }` in `protobase.config.ts`, `resolveAccess(source, ctx, { roles })`), for every resource whatever its rules. A filter is the capability's row filter, so like `.own` it applies where the capability decides: an operation without a rule, or a rule built with `roles.can(...)`.

**Several roles add up.** A user gets every field one of their roles lists (all of them when a role holds the plain capability) and the rows any of their roles allows. Fields and rows add up separately: someone holding both `erp_sync` and `reseller` above reads `name` on unpublished products too. With Better Auth a session acts with one [active role](auth.md#active-role)) at a time, so this only comes up with an authenticator that hands out several.

### Wildcards in has, can and holds

A wildcard in a role grants everything it stands for: `*.read` reads every resource. What a check asks for is different, so the checks take wildcards in one place only:

- `roles.has(user, 'vms.update')` and `roles.can('vms.update')` ask for one capability, in any scope or limit the role holds it. They refuse a wildcard, at compile time and when called, since `vms.*` would pass for a role holding only `vms.read`: ask for each capability instead.
- `roles.holds(user, 'vms.*')` asks for all of it, in every row and field: a role holding `*` or `vms.*` passes, one holding `vms.read`, `*.read`, `vms.update.own` or a `vms.update` limited to fields or rows does not. A scope asks for those rows at least: `orders.read.own` passes for a role holding `orders.read.own`, `orders.read` or `*.read`. API functions' `capability` is checked this way.

## Anonymous access

The role `anonymous` is what a request without a token acts as. A project without it answers such requests `401`, as always.

```ts
anonymous: [{ 'products.read': { fields: ['name', 'slug', 'price', 'image'], filter: 'published = true' } }],
```

- **It reads listed fields, and creates them through a public form only.** Each entry names one resource, `read` or `create` without a scope, and its fields; `defineRoles` refuses other capabilities, wildcards, `.own` and `.team`, and a capability without a field list, so nothing becomes public by accident, a new column included. A `create` is used by the resource's [public forms](forms.md)) alone, behind their rate limit and bot check: everywhere else it does not exist.
- **No token, not a bad one.** A request without an `Authorization` header is served as a caller holding only this role, in no organization. A header with anything but a valid, unexpired token is still a `401`. `jwtAuthenticator` and `betterAuthAuthenticator` tell the two apart; an authenticator of your own throws `MissingCredentials` (from `@protobase/server`) for a request without a credential to do the same.
- **Only its capabilities open anything.** The capability is ANDed into a resource's access rule, so a rule that allows everyone (`read: () => true`) or `defaultAccess: 'allow'` never lets an anonymous caller in on its own.
- **The resources API and `/api/meta` only.** Lists, records, `:search`, `:seek` and the aggregates of what the role reads, with filters, sorts and `fields` checked as for everyone: an unlisted field is refused like an unknown one. A resource it cannot read is a `404`; a write, or another operation it may not do on a resource it reads, is a `401` that asks for a token, a `create` it holds for a form included. `/api/meta` describes what it reads, for the [admin app](#browsing-the-admin-app). `/api/openapi.json`, `/api/docs`, batch writes, [API functions](../guides/api-functions.md)), the assistant and the file cleanup still need a token. A [file field](files.md#downloads)) it reads comes with its link, as for anyone.
- A tenant-scoped resource (`.tenant`) cannot be in it, since an anonymous caller works in no organization; the server refuses to start.
- Reading has no rate limit of its own: put a proxy or CDN in front of a public API to limit and cache requests. [Public forms](forms.md#rate-limit)) limit their submissions.

### Browsing the admin app

With an anonymous role that reads a resource, `GET /api/auth/status` says `"anonymous": true`, and the admin app opens for someone who is not signed in instead of the sign-in page: the sidebar, lists, displays, filters and record pages of what the role reads, read-only, with the views and pages of the role `anonymous` (a view `.forRoles(['anonymous'])` is theirs alone). The sidebar has a **Sign in** button where the profile menu would be. It opens the sign-in route, `/-/sign-in`, a page of its own: the browser's Back, or **Continue without signing in**, returns to browsing, and signing in comes back to the page it was opened from. Signing out returns to browsing. A link for the sign-in steps, such as a password reset, still opens its page. An anonymous role that only creates, for public forms, leaves the app behind sign-in.

## Use cases

One shop's catalog, read by its staff, by the warehouse system and by web store visitors. CI typechecks and tests the file:

```ts title="docs-examples/reference/catalog.ts"
import { defineRoles, f, resource } from '@protobase/schema'

// A shop's catalog, read by its staff, by the warehouse system and by visitors of the web store, who sign in to nothing.

export const roles = defineRoles<'products' | 'costs'>({
  admin: ['*'],
  editor: ['products.read', 'products.create', 'products.update'],
  buyer: ['products.read', 'costs.read'],
  // The warehouse system reads three columns and changes one. A column added later stays hidden from it.
  erp_sync: [{ 'products.read': ['sku', 'price', 'stock'] }, { 'products.update': ['stock'] }],
  // Requests without a token: what the web store shows, of published products only.
  anonymous: [{ 'products.read': { fields: ['name', 'slug', 'price', 'image'], filter: 'published = true' } }],
})

/** shop.products */
export const products = resource('products')
  .table('shop.products')
  .fields({
    id: f.integer().readOnly().filterable().sortable().dbDefault(),
    sku: f.text().filterable().sortable(),
    name: f.text().filterable().sortable(),
    slug: f.text().filterable(),
    price: f.decimal({ precision: 10, scale: 2 }).filterable().sortable(),
    // Whoever reads products, only roles holding `costs.read` see what one costs the shop.
    cost_price: f.decimal({ precision: 10, scale: 2 }).access({ read: roles.can('costs.read') }),
    stock: f.integer().filterable(),
    image: f.file().accept(['image/*']).public().optional(),
    published: f.boolean().default(false).filterable(),
  })
  .primaryKey((r) => r.id)
  .search((r) => [r.name, r.sku])
```

### A public storefront catalog

The web store lists products without signing in:

```sh
curl 'https://shop.example.com/api/v1/products?order_by=name&page_size=20'
```

Each item has `id`, `name`, `slug`, `price` and `image`, of published products only: a draft's URL is a `404`. `filter=cost_price < 10` or `order_by=stock` is a `400`, worded as an unknown field, and a `PATCH` without a token is a `401`. The staff sign in as before and see what their roles allow. A column added to `shop.products` later, such as a supplier, stays off the store until it is added to the list.

### An integration limited to some columns

`erp_sync` is a role for a system: a user with that role, and a token for it ([`issueToken`](auth.md#tokens-for-scripts-and-curl))). It reads `sku`, `price` and `stock` of every product and writes only `stock`; a `PATCH` with `price` is a `400`, as for a field it cannot see, and `cost_price` is not in its responses. A role that only uses the API needs no view: views shape the admin app, while what a caller may see and do is decided here.

### Field rules or field lists

A field rule goes from the field to the roles: `cost_price` above is hidden from every role that reads products but those holding `costs.read`. Use it for the few sensitive columns of a resource that many roles read, such as a screening result (`f.text().access({ read: roles.can('screening.read') })`). A field list goes from the role to the fields: use it for a role that should see only some columns, such as an integration or anonymous visitors, so a new column stays hidden from it. When both apply, a field needs both.

### Write-only fields

A role writes a field it cannot read only when the field's own `create` or `update` rule allows it: `f.text().access({ read: roles.is('loop'), create: roles.is('admin'), update: roles.is('admin') })` lets `admin` set a value only `loop` reads. A write rule the field follows from its resource never does, so hiding a field from a role does not let everyone who updates the resource overwrite it. The value is in no response, history, export or webhook of the writer, and no reveal shows it to them. `/meta` gives the writer the field marked `writeOnly: true`, sensitive and neither filterable nor sortable, and keeps it in the view's record sections and field hints only, so the admin app edits it only where a section of the layout names it: as a password-style input to type a new value in, with no stored value or eye to reveal one, never kept in a form's unsaved changes, and nowhere on the read view. The record's `permissions.fields` lists it as `edit` where the writer may update it. A file field, or the field a resource orders its records by (`.position()`), is never write-only, and no `reorder` orders by a write-only field.

## Records that belong to another

A record often belongs to another one through a relation, such as an operation to the VM it runs on, and who may write it follows from who may change that VM. `.parent((r) => r.vm_id, 'update')` says so: writing an operation needs `update` on the record `vm_id` points at, `'read'` needing only to see it, as for a comment on a ticket. A member below may run operations on their own VMs only, with no rule of your own:

```ts title="docs-examples/reference/child-records.ts"
import { defineRoles, f, resource } from '@protobase/schema'

// Virtual machines and the operations run on them: a member creates an operation only on a VM they may update.

export const roles = defineRoles<'vms' | 'operations'>({
  admin: ['*'],
  member: ['vms.read', 'vms.update.own', 'operations.read', 'operations.create'],
})

/** virt.vms, each owned by the user who made it. */
export const vms = resource('vms')
  .table('virt.vms')
  .fields({
    id: f.integer().readOnly().filterable().dbDefault(),
    name: f.text().filterable(),
    owner_id: f.text().readOnly().filterable(),
  })
  .primaryKey((r) => r.id)
  .owner((r) => r.owner_id)

/** virt.operations: writing one needs `update` on the VM its `vm_id` points at. */
export const operations = resource('operations')
  .table('virt.operations')
  .fields({
    id: f.integer().readOnly().filterable().dbDefault(),
    vm_id: f.relation('vms').filterable(),
    kind: f.enum(['start', 'stop', 'reboot']),
  })
  .primaryKey((r) => r.id)
  .parent((r) => r.vm_id, 'update')
```

- **Every write is checked.** Creating a record checks the parent it names; changing it, the parent it points at and the one it moves to; deleting and undeleting it, the parent it points at. So a record cannot be created under an allowed parent and then moved under another. It holds for `/api/v1` and its batches, and for everything that writes through them: forms, [API functions](../guides/api-functions.md)) and the assistant.
- **The caller's own rules decide.** The parent is read as the caller would read it, with its tenant, row filters, soft delete and record-level rules; for `update`, also its update row filter and record-level update rule, given an empty input. A parent the caller cannot see, may not update, that is soft deleted or does not exist gets the same `403` as a refused create (`You may not create this operations record`), and nothing is written: the answer does not tell which VM ids exist.
- **A null relation checks nothing.** A relation set by a column default or a trigger is checked from the record as written.
- **`update` follows the parent's own parents**, so with VMs under `.parent((r) => r.folder_id, 'update')` an operation needs update on the VM's folder too. A write that would put a record under itself, or under a cycle already in the data, is refused. A `read` parent is not followed further.
- **Several parents** are each checked with their own access, also two of one resource, such as a transfer that reads its `source_vm_id` and updates its `target_vm_id`.
- **The parent is locked until the write commits** (`FOR NO KEY UPDATE`), so a VM handed to someone else or deleted at the same moment is waited for and checked again. That is the cost: writes of records under one parent, and through an `update` parent under one ancestor, run one after another. The server's database role needs `UPDATE` on the parent's table to take the lock. Two writes that lock the same records in opposite orders, such as two batches writing under VM A then B and B then A, can deadlock: Postgres rolls one back, which answers `409` and writes nothing, and the client sends it again.
- The record page and `/api/meta` count the check, so the admin app offers no Edit or Delete the server would refuse. `/api/sb/rest/v1` does not use Protobase's access rules at all, so this check is not part of it.

## Restricted model and row filters

[`resolveAccess`](https://docs.protobase.net/api/schema/functions/resolveaccess/)) returns everything a request may do. Use [`restrictModel(model, access)`](https://docs.protobase.net/api/schema/functions/restrictmodel/)) for everything user-facing (checking filters and sorts, queries, OpenAPI, `/meta`): hidden fields are gone, so they cannot be referenced, searched, sorted or leaked. Key columns always stay, because records are addressed by them.

Row filters (`access.rowFilter`) are a separate thing. They come from the access rules (`.own`, `.team`, filters of capabilities, returned filters), are checked against the **full** model because they may use hidden or non-filterable columns, and are ANDed into queries by the server.
